## What I built this summer

<br>

- **DHSVM**, the distributed hydrology model I use for post-fire watershed work, requires a demanding input set:\
  [**gridded terrain binaries** · a **routed, ordered stream network** · **initial model states**]{.small}

- This summer that preparation became a **toolkit**:\
  [**one command**, from a **watershed boundary shapefile + DEM** to the complete input set]{.small}

- Most outputs are **not DHSVM-specific**:\
  [the **stream network** in particular serves many kinds of watershed analysis]{.small}

::: notes
About 30 seconds. Plain opening: what the model needs, what I built, and why the talk is framed around the toolkit rather than the model. At the midterm I covered the science, so today goes straight to the tool. The last sentence sets up the second half of the talk.
:::

::: notes
About 40 seconds. A DEM is elevation numbers on a grid. [advance] Each cell compares itself with its eight neighbors and asks which one is steepest downhill. Diagonal neighbors are farther away, so the comparison uses drop per unit distance. [advance] Doing this everywhere gives every cell a pointer. This is called D8 flow direction. The toolkit's engine uses a multiple-direction variant on hillslopes, which spreads flow more realistically, but the idea is the same.
:::

::: {.r-stack}
![](assets/p2_a_terrain.png){fig-align="center" height="640"}

![](assets/p2_b_rain.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height="640"}

![](assets/p2_c_acc.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height="640"}
:::

::: notes
About 45 seconds. This is a synthetic landscape, shown as a hillshade. [advance] Drop one unit of rain on every cell. [advance] Let each drop follow the arrows and count how many pass through each cell. That count is flow accumulation. Nobody drew these rivers; the valleys emerge from counting. A ridge cell has a count of one. The main channel collects thousands of cells.
:::

::: notes
About 50 seconds. One question remains: how many drops make a stream? The threshold is a support area, the amount of land that must drain into a cell before we call it a channel. [drag the slider slowly] With a large threshold only the trunk streams appear. As the threshold shrinks, channels climb up the hillslopes, and the drainage density in the corner changes by a factor of about two hundred. Every extraction tool asks for this number, and it is usually chosen by eye. The next slide shows how the toolkit chooses it instead. After dragging, click on an empty part of the slide so the arrow keys advance slides again.
:::

## Choosing the threshold objectively {.smaller}

A network extracted from a DEM depends on one free parameter, the support area A~c~. The toolkit selects it with the constant stream drop test: in a properly extracted network, first-order streams show the same mean elevation drop as higher-order streams. The sweep takes the first sustained band where the test passes (|t| < 2).

![](assets/ac_resolution_bands.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" width="72%"}

Because A~c~ is a physical area, the same value remains valid when the grid changes from 28 m to 10 m. Holding the cell count fixed instead would give a network about eight times too dense at 10 m.

::: notes
About 50 seconds. Walk the figure. The blue bars are the thresholds the drop test accepts at the two resolutions, on the same basin. They overlap, and the chosen area, 60 cells at 28 m and 476 cells at 10 m, lies in the 28 m band and at the lower edge of the 10 m band. The red mark shows the alternative: keeping 60 cells at 10 m would put channel initiation at 0.006 square kilometers, which no part of the test accepts. The criterion is stated, physical, and repeatable, which is what a methods section needs.
:::

## From channel cells to a network {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
![](assets/p4_topology.png){height="540"}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Channel cells are vectorized into segments, directed downstream, ordered from headwaters to outlet, and connected to a single outlet. Each segment carries its length, slope, drainage area, and channel class.

<br>

This topology is what routing requires, in DHSVM or any other model. It also supports transport along the network, for temperature, sediment, or nutrients, and connectivity measures for stream ecology.

<br>

[Distance ties at junctions are resolved by a fixed rule, so the same boundary gives the same network in every run.]{.muted .small}
:::

::::

::: notes
About 45 seconds. A picture of streams is not yet something you can compute on. The toolkit builds a proper directed network, and the figure shows what the watershed itself means: every cell whose water reaches this outlet. The attribute table travels in a plain shapefile. One detail for the computationally minded: junction geometry can produce exact distance ties, and the toolkit resolves them with a fixed rule, so results are reproducible run to run.
:::

## Running it on the Duke Compute Cluster {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
```bash
ssh dcc                # dcc-login.oit.duke.edu
git clone https://github.com/waveletswave/DHSVM_Stream_Toolkit_ThatWorks.git
source /hpc/group/abmurraylab/ys451/env.sh
   # Anaconda3, conda env dhsvm_geo, GRASS/7.6.0

export DHSVM_EPSG=32617
export DHSVM_WATERSHED=.../arwd_watershed_UTM17.shp
export DHSVM_DEM_SOURCE=.../AR_src_3dep_10m.tif
export DHSVM_OUT=/work/ys451/cct_demo/outputs_AR_10m
export DHSVM_STREAM_SOURCE_AREA_M2=22000
bash standalone_CA/pipeline/run_pipeline.sh
```

## Validation {.smaller}

Rebuilt against an audited reference implementation, with acceptance criteria fixed before porting: sha256 byte identity for the flat binaries, pixel-level equivalence for the rasters.

```{=html}
<div class="vlabel">STAGE BY STAGE, AGAINST THE REFERENCE</div>
<div style="display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; align-items:stretch; justify-content:center; gap:10px; margin:0.3em 0 0.5em 0;">
  <div class="vstage"><b>clip</b><span>max |&Delta;| 0.0</span></div>
  <div class="vstage"><b>slope</b><span>max |&Delta;| 0.0</span></div>
  <div class="vstage"><b>base grids</b><span>sha256 identical</span></div>
  <div class="vstage"><b>hydrology</b><span>max |&Delta;| 0.0</span></div>
  <div class="vstage doc"><b>soil depth</b><span>1 float32 ULP</span><em>documented</em></div>
  <div class="vstage doc"><b>stream network</b><span>2 junction ties</span><em>documented</em></div>
  <div class="vstage"><b>model states</b><span>sha256 identical</span></div>
</div>
<div class="vlabel">END TO END</div>
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; gap:72px; margin:0.4em 0 0.8em 0;">
  <div class="stat"><div class="n">NSE 0.99999510</div><div class="l">hourly streamflow, 2016 to 2018,<br>standalone vs reference</div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="n">PBIAS &minus;0.000059%</div><div class="l">same three years,<br>same comparison</div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="n">identical</div><div class="l">skill scores against<br>observed streamflow</div></div>
</div>
```

[The two amber stages are recorded in the validation log with cause and consequence: a math-library rounding difference of one bit, and one geometrically undefined tie resolved by the fixed rule.]{.muted .small}

::: notes
About 40 seconds. The habit worth taking away: decide what counts as the same before rewriting anything, separately for each output type. Binaries have no excuse, so the standard is byte identity. Rasters legitimately differ in their containers, so the standard is the pixels. Five stages are exact. The two amber ones could not be exact for reasons that are themselves instructive: one difference lives below the algorithm in the math library, and one is a genuinely undefined tie. Both are in the validation log. The bottom row is the end-to-end result.
:::

## Uses beyond DHSVM {.smaller}

Everything upstream of the DHSVM writers is general. Uses I can see directly:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.usecard}
**Stream ecology and habitat.** Network distance, fragmentation, and connectivity, computed from the directed network and its attribute table.
:::

::: {.usecard}
**Water quality and temperature.** A defined downstream order for routing along the channel network.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.usecard}
**Geomorphology and erosion.** Longitudinal profiles, knickpoints, and slope against drainage area from the same rasters.
:::

::: {.usecard}
**Other hydrologic models.** The same terrain and stream products; only a small writer for the target format is needed.
:::
:::

::::

<br>

The repository is public under an MIT license and includes a step-by-step guide for a new watershed. I am glad to help anyone who wants to try it on their own basin.

::: notes
About 50 seconds. This is why the talk spent its middle on principles rather than on DHSVM file formats. The general outputs are standard GeoTIFFs and a shapefile, so they drop into R, Python, or any GIS without conversion. Walk the four cards briefly. Close with the offer as stated on the slide.
:::
